# System Evaluation and Red-Teaming {#sec-evaluating-agentic-architect}

::: {.epigraph}
> "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure."
>
> — Marilyn Strathern, "'Improving Ratings': Audit in the British University System" [@Strathern1997Goodhart, p. 308]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *How should the complete AI-native system be measured, compared, and deliberately challenged?*

**Core thesis:** *Evaluation must separate the candidate design, a method or component, the configured technical system, and the complete human-plus-technical workflow through matched baselines, total cost accounting, and adversarial red-teaming.*
:::

An AI-native design system can synthesize an impressive-looking Verilog module or close timing on a synthetic benchmark and still fail as an industrial engineering workflow. Suppose an automated system reaches 5% lower latency than a tuned conventional flow, but only after senior engineers spend weeks triaging its failed candidates and running up a compute bill the conventional flow never incurred. Once that effort and compute are counted, the new workflow may not have improved the project at all. Evaluation must determine whether an automated system delivers better architectural results, lower total cost at the same quality, or both when compared against a strong alternative, which is often a well-tuned conventional baseline.

Even when individual representations, surrogates, or checks transfer across design problems (@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack), the recurring failure in complete-system evaluation is crediting the wrong source of a gain. A pass rate earned by one lucky sample from a large language model (LLM), or a timing improvement driven by a human-written wrapper, is too easily reported as the capability of the whole system. An evaluation therefore begins by naming which of four objects a claim is about (@fig-ch10-cover-map): the candidate design, a method or component, the configured technical system, or the complete human-plus-technical workflow. It then compares that object against a matched alternative, accounts for total cost ($C_{\text{workflow}} = \langle C_{\text{compute}}, C_{\text{license}}, C_{\text{human}} \rangle$), and tests the result against benchmark contamination, proxy gaming, and constraint tampering.

![**Evaluating complete claims across four distinct objects.** Rigorous evaluation separates candidate designs, methods or components, configured technical systems, and complete human-plus-technical workflows. Matched comparisons against non-learned baselines and deliberate stress testing produce qualified claims that bound performance and cost without preempting commitment decisions.](images/ch10-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch10-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which evaluation distinguishes the object, four judgments, a matched alternative, deliberate challenges, and a qualified claim that is not a commitment."}

## Defining the Complete Design System Under Test {#sec-evaluation-objects}

Validating one of those four objects does not validate the others. A synthesized register-transfer level (RTL) module that passes its checks neither proves that a learned method caused the pass nor shows that the complete workflow saved engineering time. When an automated synthesis loop produces a better floorplan, it is tempting to credit the generative model, yet a simulated-annealing placer or a human-written verification wrapper may have done the real work while the model merely supplied starting seeds at high inference cost.

A fair comparison separates the candidate design from the software that generated it and from the workflow that produced it, because a measurement can describe any one of the three. Every evaluation must therefore state which of four distinct objects it is testing:

1. **Candidate design artifacts:** the hardware and software deliverables produced during a study, including synthesizable register-transfer level (RTL) modules, intermediate representations, microarchitecture parameter configurations, floorplans, instruction set architecture (ISA) extensions, and firmware routines.
2. **Methods and components:** individual algorithmic building blocks within the system, such as a foundation model generator, a learned graph surrogate for wirelength or timing, a Bayesian optimization loop, or an automated retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline.
3. **Configured technical systems:** the software-and-tool ensemble operating autonomously without human intervention, including the orchestrator, tool interfaces, domain models, execution containers, local memory state, and verification checks.
4. **Complete human-plus-technical workflows:** the entire engineering process deployed on an architectural program, including human architects, prompt engineers, domain experts, external tool dependencies, review boards, and interactive escalation paths.

These four evaluation objects are independent of the operational layers defined in @sec-three-operational-layers. While the object names what a claim evaluates, the operational layer sets the allowed action space, the depth of verification required, and the failure modes that can invalidate a run. At Layer 1, a point-assistance tool can be evaluated as a component, its generated RTL as a candidate design, and its use by an engineer as a complete workflow, although functional pass rates on isolated modules (such as `pass@k` on VerilogEval) say nothing about downstream integration effort or physical feasibility. At Layer 2, a parameter search scored on surrogate power, performance, and area (PPA) estimates (such as analytical wirelength or fast cycle simulators) inside a fixed hardware template can expose bottlenecks that the model captures, but cannot fix bottlenecks that require changing the template itself. At Layer 3, a claim requires system-level evidence across cross-layer PPA effects, functional correctness under formal contracts, and the physical checks demanded by its scope, as the public Design Conductor reports partially illustrate (@sec-design-conductor-case). Giving a system more degrees of freedom requires deeper checks matched to what it can change, without blurring candidate, component, system, and workflow claims or assuming that evidence for one automatically covers the others.

### Freezing the System Under Test {#sec-freezing-system-under-test}

When prompts, retry budgets, retrieval corpora, or synthesis scripts drift between runs, a study can easily credit the wrong source of a gain: a team might attribute a $12\%$ timing-closure improvement to a new base model when an engineer also widened the retry limit and relaxed a synthesis constraint mid-study. Because base models, tool access, feedback loops, and human-written wrappers all change outcomes [@WangEtAl2026ArchEval], retry rules, retrieved documents, prompts, and search policies are working parts of a configured system or complete workflow; naming only the model hides the actual engineering system under test. Before measuring whether one workflow beats another, the evaluation protocol must therefore name the object under test, freeze the system identity, and define its allowed action space so that every benchmark score remains tied to what the comparison held fixed and what it varied. Freezing that identity fixes the rules governing a run while still allowing the design state, generated prompts, and retrieved material to evolve under those recorded rules.

The allowed action space determines both what a score means and how a run can fail or cheat:

- **RTL or intermediate-representation generation.** The system produces a new design artifact, and the evaluation checks functional correctness, blocking constraints, physical feasibility, structural soundness, and maintenance effort.
- **Tool, script, or parameter tuning.** The system modifies analysis or implementation parameters. The evaluation must specify which settings may change, log their initial and chosen values, and hold the top-level requirements, independent acceptance checks, and stopping rules fixed so that relaxed test conditions are not mistaken for hardware improvements.
- **Microarchitecture change.** The system modifies CPU core structures, neural processing unit (NPU) tensor arrays, cache hierarchies, Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) chiplet interfaces, or thermal throttling limits. Checking these changes across multi-tool environments (such as comparing RTL simulation in Verilator or Synopsys VCS against FireSim) requires testing the affected workloads, software stacks, physical implementations, and integration boundaries.
- **Test or constraint change.** The system modifies a testbench, formal property, timing constraint, or scoring script. Independent, evaluator-owned checks must verify that the system under test cannot weaken or bypass its own requirements.

This fourth action space needs a clear boundary before an experiment begins. Top-level requirements and final acceptance checks must remain fixed and owned by the evaluator, even when the system under test is allowed to propose changes to internal design constraints for independent verification. For example, a two-cycle arithmetic unit may legitimately need an internal multicycle timing exception once an independent formal check confirms that the control logic never captures data on the first cycle, but that exception cannot lower the target clock frequency or relax the external interface contract. Freezing the evaluation therefore locks down both the top-level requirements and the rule for approving internal constraint changes, without forbidding every edit to a candidate's constraint file.

Because RTL pass rates, parameter-tuning PPA scores, and microarchitectural workload speedups come from different action spaces with different verification depths and ways to game a metric, a fair comparison must log every system feature that can alter capability, cost, or interpretation (@tbl-complete-system-identity). Two workflows built around the same base model are different systems if they use different retrieval corpora, wrappers, retry budgets, or tool interfaces.

| **Element** | **What the record must identify** | **Why it matters** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Evaluation object** | Candidate design, method/component, configured technical system, or complete human-plus-technical workflow | Results can only be interpreted at the specific level evaluated. |
| **Learned components** | Immutable model snapshot or endpoint identity, access date, mutable alias if used, inference settings, and fine-tuning | Modifying models or settings creates a different system; aliases obscure exact runs. |
| **Design information** | Starting artifacts, retrieved sources with versions, represented state, retrieval coverage, conflict handling, and update policies | Extra or fresher information can explain apparent capability gains. |
| **Methods and instructions** | Selected generation, prediction, optimization, or other methods and their composition rules; system/task instructions; prompt policy; routing policy | Models are components in broader procedures; changing instructions or policies changes the evaluated setup. |
| **Legal action space** | Permitted design, tool, script, parameter, test, and constraint modifications | Allowed actions dictate supported claims and potential evaluation manipulation. |
| **System tool interfaces** | Tool wrappers/schemas, wrapper revision, available executable tools, and permitted calls | Interfaces determine possible actions and visible failures. |
| **Task and evaluation environments** | Task requirements and workloads; tool versions, configurations, checkpoints, dependencies, containers, and recorded outputs | Changed tasks or evaluation conditions can explain changed results. |
| **Checks** | Functional, architectural, physical, security, and acceptance checks; ownership and rules for admitting internal changes | Results are only as strong as cleared verification checks. |
| **Human work** | Setup, prompting, intervention, review, repair, and escalation roles | Hidden engineering effort makes automated results appear artificially cheap. |
| **Operating limits** | Compute, tool, time, retry, and review budgets plus stopping rules | Differences in budgets or access must be accounted for in the comparison. |
: **A complete-workflow identity extends well beyond the model.** The record distinguishes the evaluation object and renders every material source of capability and cost visible. {#tbl-complete-system-identity tbl-colwidths="[22,40,38]"}

Because a cryptographic hash or version string names an artifact without preserving its contents, the practical test of an evaluation record is whether another engineer can replay the run. The study must retain the prompts, retrieved documents, starting artifacts, scripts, constraints, workloads, containers, and raw logs needed to rebuild the experiment, alongside each candidate's deliverables (such as synthesizable RTL or a simulator configuration), parameter mappings, and frozen tool settings. Retaining these files lets a reviewer re-run the experiment and check whether the reported numbers hold up, though it does not remove run-to-run tool variation, which the reliability analysis measures separately. When an external model provider does not expose immutable weight snapshots, the record must log the endpoint name and access dates while noting that neither guarantees the exact same model weights served every request, making bit-exact replay impossible from that log alone.

The eight Lighthouse domains introduced in @sec-intent-vs-spec, from workload selection to verification, help teams separate environmental conditions from the system identity itself. Recording the task and tool environment separately from the system under test clarifies which comparisons remain valid when a tool version or workload changes, preventing two common mistakes: crediting a base model for capabilities provided by its tool environment, and comparing percentage gains measured on different tasks, tool setups, or physical design stages.

### The Four Evaluation Judgments {#sec-four-evaluation-judgments}

Even after the system and its environment are frozen, no single number can show that an AI-native system improves architecture work. Folding design quality, tool coordination, compute cost, and run-to-run stability into a single scalar score hides critical engineering trade-offs. Because a design must satisfy its hard constraints before secondary gains count at all, a $15\%$ increase in instructions per cycle (IPC) cannot make up for a 250\ ps violation of a required hold-time bound at a receiving register, where metastability prevents the hardware from operating reliably under the checked conditions.[^fn-hold-metastability-c10] Evaluation therefore keeps four judgments separate so readers can see which engineering decisions a measurement supports and what it leaves unanswered (@tbl-evaluation-metric-map).

[^fn-hold-metastability-c10]: **Hold-time violation and metastability**: A hold-time violation occurs when an input data signal changes too quickly after the active clock edge, violating the flip-flop's required internal stabilization window. This failure mode can trap the bistable storage element in an indeterminate metastable state between logic 0 and 1 for an unbounded duration, causing catastrophic functional breakdown in downstream logic that cannot be recovered by lowering the clock frequency.

| **Decision question** | **Concrete measures** | **Workflow insight** | **What metric cannot establish alone** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Is the architecture result supported?** | Function and blocking constraints; latency/throughput; power/thermal; area/cost; security; feasibility; maintainability; integration burden | Candidate achievement, requirements met, and verification depth | Whether AI improved engineering work, result repeatability, or commitment justification |
| **Did the workflow make sound decisions?** | Component selection; state consistency; tool/fidelity selection; interpretation accuracy; explanation faithfulness; decision usefulness; false accepts/rejects; escalation/recovery | Coordination quality, tool output interpretation, and evidence-backed decision making | Objective design adequacy, economic viability, or advantage stability under shift |
| **What was the total cost?** | Model tokens/calls; compiler builds; simulation, formal, and physical runs; compute/memory/licenses; setup/data; retries; elapsed time; human engineering | Resource expenditure and cost shifting | Candidate correctness or specific component attribution |
| **Is the advantage reliable?** | Repeated runs; calibration; worst cases; recovery; sensitivity to seeds, prompts, workloads, tools, and corners | Advantage recurrence rate and tested condition envelope | Structural reason for advantage or transferability beyond tested scope |
: **Evaluation metrics support distinct engineering decisions.** Architecture results take precedence; coordination, cost, and reliability explain how results were achieved. Red-team tests cut across all four rows. {#tbl-evaluation-metric-map tbl-colwidths="[22,30,22,26]"}

These four rows cannot trade off against one another: sound workflow decisions can still yield weak designs if the search space is poor, a strong winning design can hide a wasteful workflow, and low total cost never excuses a broken timing or functional constraint. Within the second row, explanation faithfulness checks whether a generated rationale matches the recorded tool outputs, whereas a directional intervention (such as transposing a workload matrix or swapping a floorplan aspect ratio) tests whether the stated mechanism actually predicts how the hardware metrics move. If the metric shifts in the opposite direction, the proposed mechanism is wrong even if the text quoted the original log numbers accurately. Decision-usefulness and prompt-stability checks likewise test whether explanations help human reviewers and stay consistent when prompts are rephrased, though none of these coordination checks proves hardware quality or low cost on its own.

Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM)[^fn-helm-c10] established the practice of reporting multiple metrics across multiple scenarios rather than crowning a single leaderboard winner [@LiangEtAl2023HELM], and the four judgments bring that discipline to hardware design. The protocol in @sec-minimum-complete-workflow-protocol turns those four judgments into a concrete experiment: it pairs claims with the tool fidelity needed to test them, locks down evaluator-owned checks so the system under test cannot edit them, tracks both human and machine cost across comparison arms, and tests benchmark integrity against trivial baselines and state leakage (@sec-benchmark-health-standardization). Component-level diagnostics such as surrogate calibration, generator diversity, and optimizer regret remain useful for finding bottlenecks inside a pipeline, but they do not replace end-to-end measurements of the resulting hardware and the complete workflow.

[^fn-helm-c10]: **Holistic Evaluation of Language Models**: HELM established multi-metric, multi-scenario evaluation protocols designed to capture trade-offs across accuracy, robustness, calibration, and computational efficiency in foundation models.

### Complete-Workflow Protocol {#sec-minimum-complete-workflow-protocol}

Informal workflow comparisons easily go off the rails when evaluation steps run out of order: teams tune prompts directly on test benchmarks, drop timed-out place-and-route runs from cost averages, or stop at cycle-level simulation while claiming silicon-ready gains. The eight-step protocol below prevents those shortcuts when comparing an AI-native workflow against a conventional baseline. It fixes what is being compared, sets the acceptance criteria before any runs begin, logs both passing and failing attempts, and requires every candidate check to reach the tool fidelity demanded by the claim (a simulator-level study need not run place-and-route, whereas a claim of manufacturable silicon must pass physical implementation checks).

1. Freeze both workflows along with their configured technical systems, tool environments, task sets, allowed actions, evaluator-owned checks, and artifact versions.
2. Declare the primary architecture metrics, blocking constraints, design margins, resource budgets, stopping rules, and failure handling rules before running the experiment.
3. Balance or randomize paired tasks and human operators across arms, keeping a held-out test set strictly separate from prompt and hyperparameter tuning.
4. Run both complete workflows and emit structured execution records (@sec-execution-records) for every attempt on every assigned task.
5. Promote candidates through the tool-fidelity stages required by the claim, checking cheap screening proxies against independent higher-fidelity tools. For a physical implementation claim, these checks test whether Pareto-optimal rankings survive dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) thermal throttling and voltage-drop ($IR$-drop) guardbands.[^fn-ir-drop-c10]
6. Estimate paired task-level outcome and cost differences with uncertainty bounds that account for failed runs, timeouts, and task-to-task variation.
7. Run the declared sensitivity, component-ablation, benchmark-integrity, robustness, fault-injection, and red-team tests with equal budgets across arms.
8. Report each claim as supported, unsupported, or unresolved alongside the tasks, environmental conditions, total costs, and scope limits that govern the result.

[^fn-ir-drop-c10]: **IR-drop guardbands**: In high-performance silicon, resistive voltage drop ($IR$ drop) along the power distribution network degrades effective supply voltage at standard-cell inputs, slowing switching speeds. Guardbands insert operating margins into static timing constraints to accommodate dynamic supply fluctuations under peak current draw and thermal throttling, preventing timing failures at worst-case operating corners.

Every reported metric in step 8 must state what was measured, across which tasks, under which evaluator-owned checks, within what budget, and using which aggregation rule. Statistical estimates must also name the experimental unit so that four nested levels of activity are never confused:

1. **Execution attempts:** individual tries at fulfilling a tool or model request, including retries and crashed or timed-out jobs. A single attempt may launch several backend jobs or fail before any tool starts, and it may produce logs or measurements without yielding a valid design candidate.
2. **Generated candidates:** distinct design artifacts or parameter configurations proposed for a task. A single candidate may go through several verification attempts, but those checks do not make it multiple candidates.
3. **Complete workflow runs:** end-to-end executions of the full human-plus-technical workflow on an assigned task, each of which may span many attempts and many candidates.
4. **Independent tasks or design decisions:** the distinct architecture problems across which the study tests for a workflow advantage. Running the workflow ten times on the same benchmark task measures run-to-run variance on that one task; it does not create ten independent tasks.

Raw logs, traces, and tool outputs record what happened inside these four levels, but counting log lines does not increase the sample size of an experiment. Treating multiple random seeds, retry attempts, candidate samples, or tool calls from a single task as if they were independent design tasks is *pseudoreplication* [@Hurlbert1984Pseudoreplication].[^fn-pseudo-c10] In `pass@k`, for instance, drawing $k$ candidate samples estimates the probability of solving one task within $k$ tries, not performance across $k$ independent tasks [@Chen2021Codex].

[^fn-pseudo-c10]: **Pseudoreplication**: A statistical trap where correlated observations (such as multiple stochastic runs or variations generated from a single design template) are mistakenly analyzed as independent data points, artificially inflating statistical confidence and producing spuriously narrow confidence intervals.

## Judging Artifact Quality at the Right Tool Fidelity {#sec-qualifying-scoping-result}

Once the experimental units and protocol are fixed, the first of the four judgments asks whether the architectural result itself is sound. An evaluation is only as strong as the match between its measurement tools and the claim the study makes. In a Layer 1 point-assistance task, module-level checks such as `pass@k` on an RTL benchmark or abstract syntax tree (AST) linting confirm that a generated block compiles and passes its unit testbench; that is enough to judge local code completion, but it says nothing about physical timing closure or the effort needed to integrate the block into a full system-on-chip (SoC). Layer 2 parameter sweeps go a step further by using fast cycle-level simulators or analytical wirelength models to search inside a fixed hardware template. Those proxies speed up exploration and can expose bottlenecks that the simulator models, such as a saturated memory bus, but they remain blind to routing congestion and cannot alter a frozen bus interface outside the allowed parameter space. A simulator-based study can legitimately stop at cycle counts if its claim stays scoped to microarchitectural behavior under that simulator. As soon as a study at any layer claims manufacturable silicon, however, fast turnaround cannot make up for failed equivalence checks or shorted power rails: beyond design rule checking (DRC) and static timing analysis (STA), candidates must pass layout versus schematic (LVS) equivalence, power-grid integrity checks (dynamic $IR$-drop and $L \cdot di/dt$ inductive droop), and electromigration (EM) current-density limits. At every scope, hard functional invariants and blocking constraints come first. A candidate that violates a hold-time bound, deadlocks a coherence protocol, or exceeds the 3\ W thermal limit fails, no matter how much it improves another metric.

Suppose a generated RTL block posts a high IPC gain in a cycle-level simulator. Running that same RTL through synthesis and place-and-route under a 3\ nm process design kit (PDK) may reveal severe routing congestion and negative timing slack that the cycle simulator never modeled.[^fn-negative-slack-c10] Worse, an automated optimization script might report zero timing slack only because it quietly added spurious `set_false_path` exceptions to the Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) file, instructing the timer to ignore the failing critical paths. The first failure calls for a higher-fidelity physical tool; the second requires checking that the evaluation constraints themselves were not tampered with. Both show why a headline number means nothing apart from the checks that verified it.

[^fn-negative-slack-c10]: **Negative slack**: For a setup check in static timing analysis, slack is the required arrival time minus the actual arrival time. Negative setup slack means the signal arrives too late to meet that check, so the result does not establish operation at the target clock frequency under the checked conditions.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Prioritize Soundness Over Tool Credit"}
**The principle:** Verify the candidate properties required by the stated architecture claim independently before crediting the design system with that result.

**The application:** Apply the same eligibility checks to both comparison arms, retain rejected candidates and their costs, and keep claims within the completed evaluation stage. A supported rejection or tie can be an architecture result; physical feasibility requires its own evidence.
:::

To keep claims within the evidence that supports them, an evaluation separates pass/fail eligibility criteria, primary architectural objectives, implementation depth, and long-term maintenance costs. The categories below illustrate what a study record must track, depending on the scope of its claim:

- **Correctness and blocking constraints:** functional verification of instruction set architecture (ISA) contracts (RV64GCV), bus protocols (Advanced eXtensible Interface 5 (AXI5), UCIe), physical design rule checking (DRC), layout versus schematic (LVS), dynamic $IR$-drop, electromigration, and thermal limits (3\ W thermal design power (TDP)).
- **Architectural objectives:** workload throughput (XRBench, SPEC CPU2017, MLPerf), compiler fusion efficiency, vectorization overhead, interconnect energy per bit, and passive thermal dissipation.
- **Implementation feasibility:** deepest cleared tool stage, spanning gem5/Verilator simulation, Triton/Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) compilation, Yosys/Design Compiler synthesis, OpenROAD/Innovus place-and-route, OpenSTA/PrimeTime timing closure, and Yosys EQY / Cadence Conformal equivalence checking under the process and library conditions declared for the study. For an illustrative 3\ nm-class low-power target, the available process data and tool support determine which of these checks can actually run.
- **Maintainability and future change cost:** code readability, interface clarity, design guideline adherence, and change cost under standard engineering change order (ECO) exercises.[^fn-eco-c10]
- **Integration and verification burden:** bus protocol compliance, assertion clarity, and downstream verification debug overhead.

[^fn-eco-c10]: **Engineering change orders**: An ECO is a localized modification to an integrated circuit late in the physical design cycle, designed to fix timing violations or functional bugs without re-running full synthesis and place-and-route from scratch. In evaluation, testing whether a system can perform ECO-style incremental repairs prevents over-optimizing for clean-slate generation while ignoring the iterative reality of chip signoff.

Because these tools and checks do not form a single linear pipeline, the evaluation record must state explicitly which checks passed and which were never run; completing place-and-route, for instance, does not by itself prove logical equivalence between the netlist and the original RTL.

Where valid candidates trade off competing objectives such as latency, power, and area, those trade-offs belong on explicit Pareto fronts [@Deb2001MultiObjective]. If a study uses a scalar weight formula to pick a single winner, publishing the weights alongside the raw uncombined metrics lets readers see what that formula rewards and penalizes. Power and energy claims likewise require explicit measurement windows, completed workload units, duty cycles, leakage states, and chip boundaries following the measurement discipline of MLPerf Power [@TschandEtAl2024MLPerfPower], since an isolated simulator estimate never establishes implementation-ready power efficiency on its own.

## Evaluating Loop Coordination and Decision Quality {#sec-coordination-decision-quality}

Verifying a candidate design shows what the hardware achieves within its tested scope, but it does not explain how the workflow navigated the search space to get there. An AI-native workflow does more than emit candidate code: it coordinates the design loop by choosing which component runs next, filtering the context that component sees, picking the right tool and simulation fidelity, folding tool results back into the shared design state, and deciding when to stop or ask a human architect for help. Even when every individual generator, surrogate, and simulator works as intended, the overall system can fail if its orchestrator coordinates those steps poorly.

Evaluating that coordination requires reconstructing the chain of consequential design decisions across a run. At each decision point, the execution log should record the engineering question at hand, the design state visible to the system, the action chosen, the expected hardware outcome, the actual tool output, how the system interpreted that output, and what it decided to do next. Capturing this decision trail does not mean hoarding every internal token or unparsed chain of thought from a language model; it means preserving enough engineering context to show why the system modified a candidate or stopped searching.

Tracing these decision chains exposes six recurring coordination failures in automated architecture workflows:

1. **Role-selection failures** occur when the workflow calls a generative model for a job that called for a deterministic table lookup, a calibrated surrogate, a mathematical optimizer, a formal equivalence checker, or a human architect's judgment.
2. **State failures** occur when the orchestration harness drops, duplicates, or scrambles design constraints, candidate IDs, tool exit statuses, physical units, or earlier simulation numbers across candidates.
3. **Information-use failures** occur when retrieval steps miss critical specification clauses, pull an outdated intellectual property (IP) revision, hide conflicting datasheet numbers, or fetch text that does not actually support the downstream design change.
4. **Tool-selection failures** occur when the workflow launches the wrong tool fidelity or repeats a run that cannot answer the question. Running a 48-hour gate-level simulation[^fn-gls-c10] in Synopsys VCS or Cadence Xcelium is a waste of compute and licenses if a fast analytical model or a Verilator trace already shows that the tile buffer is bottlenecked on memory bandwidth. While that RTL trace can diagnose the bandwidth stall, proving that the fix routes cleanly still requires physical implementation tools.
5. **Interpretation failures** occur when a tool exits cleanly, but the workflow misreads the output log, treats an inconclusive bounded proof as a full pass, or credits an IPC improvement to the wrong microarchitectural change.
6. **Control failures** occur when the workflow should halt, roll back a broken edit, or escalate to a human reviewer, but instead pushes ahead and commits a corrupted design state.

[^fn-gls-c10]: **Gate-level simulation**: Unlike cycle-accurate or RTL simulation, gate-level simulation models the structural netlist of interconnected standard cells using timing delays extracted into a Standard Delay Format (SDF) file. This verifies that the synthesized hardware functions correctly in the presence of real wire delays, setup and hold margins, clock skew, and reset glitches.

Separating tool execution, hardware observation, and decision quality prevents a common reporting mistake. A tool job that exits with status zero does not guarantee a meaningful hardware measurement, and a clean measurement does not guarantee that the workflow made a sensible next move. An evaluation must track all three: tool completion rates, false accepts (where the workflow promotes a broken candidate), and false rejects (where it throws away a candidate that independent checks later show was viable). Parser bugs, stale cached numbers, truncated traces, and state-handoff errors belong in the same log because they corrupt the evidence that later steps rely on.

Consider two retries during the same exploration run. The first retry happens after an electronic design automation (EDA) license server times out and simply resubmits the exact same synthesis job; the second happens after a formal coherence check fails and submits a cache-controller patch that fixes the wrong state transition. A raw retry counter lumps both together, even though the first is an infrastructure hiccup and the second is a reasoning failure by the design loop. Tool usage should therefore be broken down by root cause, tracking the fraction of valid tool calls, useful measurements per call, first-try versus retry success across failure types, redundant tool runs, adherence to stopping rules, escalation accuracy, human takeovers, and clean state rollbacks. Each rate needs its own valid denominator: stopping-rule compliance is measured only over runs that hit a stopping condition, escalation accuracy only over pre-labeled test cases, and state recovery only when a fault actually required a rollback, while the compute and license hours spent on those calls feed into total cost accounting (@sec-total-cost-accounting).

Retrieved specifications and IP documentation require the same audit trail. The evaluation record must log which document version was fetched, whether it contained the facts needed for the decision, and whether conflicting sources were flagged. While an ablation study can show that turning on retrieval changed the final floorplan or cache configuration, only a provenance check can verify whether the retrieved datasheet was current, complete, and applied accurately.

Judging whether the workflow made good choices requires comparing its actions against predeclared reference decisions or independent reviews by senior architects. Where reasonable architects disagree on the best next step, the evaluation should report inter-reviewer agreement and list the viable alternatives rather than forcing a single ground-truth label. For narrower prediction tasks inside the loop, standard statistical diagnostics provide three sharp checks: confidence calibration, strictly proper scoring rules,[^fn-scoring-rules-c10] and risk-coverage curves. Take a binary prediction task, such as forecasting whether a candidate accelerator block will close timing under an evaluator-owned STA check within a fixed budget. If the predictor is well calibrated, roughly $80\%$ of the held-out candidates to which it assigns an $80\%$ pass probability will actually close timing under the tested conditions [@GuoEtAl2017Calibration]. A strictly proper scoring rule rewards the model for reporting its true probability estimate rather than gaming the threshold [@GneitingRaftery2007ScoringRules], while risk-coverage curves show how the error rate drops as the system abstains on uncertain candidates and escalates them to a tool or human reviewer [@ElYanivWiener2010SelectiveClassification]. If a workflow does not output calibrated probabilities, its escalation policy should be evaluated directly by measuring false accepts and escalation load rather than inventing a synthetic confidence score. Useful as these statistical checks are for auditing decisions inside the loop, they never substitute for verifying that the final hardware works.

[^fn-scoring-rules-c10]: **Strictly proper scoring rules**: In probabilistic forecasting, a scoring rule assigns a numerical penalty to a predicted probability distribution relative to the observed outcome. A rule is strictly proper (such as the Brier score) if and only if the expected penalty is uniquely minimized by asserting the true probability distribution, preventing predictive models from gaming confidence metrics.

Finally, human intervention is part of the workflow under test, not free background support. If a senior verification engineer spends forty hours patching broken instruction-decoder logic, fixing SDC timing exceptions, and debugging memory-consistency failures produced by an automated generator, calling the result "autonomous synthesis" hides the human labor that made the chip work. Every evaluation must log when and why engineers supplied missing architectural context, corrected misread tool logs, overrode floorplan choices, patched broken RTL, or killed diverging search runs. Alongside core intervention metrics (the share of decisions needing human help, manual override rates, recovery rates after an intervention, and final hardware quality after an override), linking each intervention to the state before and after the engineer stepped in shows what the automation could not handle on its own. Pairing that intervention log with a full time and resource log reveals whether the system genuinely saved engineering effort or merely shifted human work from writing RTL to debugging prompts, fixing SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA), writing ECO patches, and cleaning up unroutable pin assignments.

## Total Design Cost Accounting {#sec-total-cost-accounting}

Because human interventions, tool retries, and dead-end explorations all consume engineering hours and schedule time, a speedup inside one step of the loop does not prove that the complete workflow saved resources if downstream debugging and verification eat up the gains. Honest evaluation keeps human engineering time, model inference and training compute, EDA tool runtime, license occupancy, energy use, and wall-clock schedule in separate accounts unless an explicit, well-justified conversion rule combines them. It likewise separates one-time setup and training costs from per-task execution costs, and active machine runtime from queue wait times. Building a custom graph surrogate, writing tool wrappers, or curating a domain dataset carries an upfront cost that must be amortized over a stated number of real design tasks: a system that pays off across two hundred block explorations can easily lose to a conventional human-driven flow on a project that needs only ten. Recording every attempt and stating the amortization horizon explicitly lets a study weigh total cost directly against the quality of the final architecture.

Consider what an architectural decision actually costs on an industrial team. The bill is never just the runtime of the final passing synthesis job; it includes weeks of engineer time spent debugging broken testbenches, cloud GPU charges for thousands of discarded candidate runs, and commercial EDA license tokens tied up overnight by parallel simulations.[^fn-eda-licenses-c10] Comparing the few seconds of model inference that produced a winning candidate against a human engineer's entire work week leaves almost the whole cost of the automated workflow off the books.

[^fn-eda-licenses-c10]: **EDA license tokens**: Commercial silicon design tools (such as Synopsys Design Compiler or Cadence Innovus) are metered through centralized floating license servers. Each active process checks out a cryptographic token; when the token pool is exhausted, subsequent jobs stall in queues or abort. In automated exploration, an unconstrained loop can lock up corporate license pools, imposing schedule delays and financial costs on neighboring engineering teams.

To measure workflow efficiency fairly, cost accounting must start when the task is assigned and run until the comparison reaches its declared endpoint, whether that endpoint is a simulator-backed recommendation, a documented rejection, or physical signoff, while charging each arm its fair share of upfront setup, model training, and data preparation. Projected downstream maintenance and ECO costs belong in a separate scenario analysis rather than mixed into observed run costs. As @tbl-total-system-cost makes clear, counting LLM tokens captures only a sliver of what an architecture exploration actually spends.

| **Cost class** | **Examples to record** |
| --- | --- |
| **Human setup** | Formulation, artifact preparation, environment integration, prompt and procedure development |
| **Human operation** | Supervision, intervention, failure triage, and manual design work |
| **Human review and decision work** | Independent checking, design review, documentation, approval preparation, and unresolved follow-up |
| **Model and general compute** | Model calls and tokens, inference time, accelerator time, training or adaptation, memory, storage, energy, and orchestration |
| **Engineering tools** | Compiler builds; invocations by tool type, fidelity, and status; simulation runs and cycles; formal, synthesis, physical, field-programmable gate array (FPGA) / emulation, and lab measurements; license peak concurrency limits, token checkout duration, queue denial wait latency, and backoff throttling |
| **Data and samples** | Workload traces, training/adaptation data, reference outputs, implementation samples, and silicon measurements |
| **Verification and integration** | Check development, proof and simulation work, debug, interface and software integration, regressions, and closing evidence |
| **Future change and ECO work** | Expected design edits, affected modules/interfaces, verification reruns, implementation work, and review for declared scenarios |
| **Failure and recovery** | Invalid candidates, repeated runs, rollback, restored state, debugging, and rework |
| **Schedule** | Wall-clock time, time to a supported decision, critical-path delay, and completion-time variability |
: **Total cost includes all work performed before, during, and after automated search within the declared accounting boundary.** Categories must be reported separately unless a disclosed accounting rule converts them into a common, justified unit. {#tbl-total-system-cost tbl-colwidths="[26,74]"}

### Execution Records and Candidate Flow {#sec-execution-records-candidate-flow}

When benchmark scripts log only winning finalists, six-hour place-and-route timeouts and crashed synthesis runs vanish from the cost account, and a single candidate retried five times after license stalls looks like five distinct hardware designs. Tallying the cost classes of @tbl-total-system-cost accurately therefore requires logging every execution attempt and linking it to its workflow run, candidate ID, configuration, and random seed, while retaining partial outputs, timeout limits, and the compute and licenses burned by failed jobs. As established in @sec-minimum-complete-workflow-protocol, a job that times out and is retried counts as two attempts on the same candidate rather than two independent designs.

Recording resources at the attempt level separates the cost of exploring new hardware ideas from the cost of nursing flaky infrastructure. Extending the operational log with the comparison arm, tool-fidelity stage, resource consumption, and linked human minutes (@tbl-attempt-cost-record) keeps failed attempts, tool crashes, and manual repair sessions on the bill even when they never produce a finalist. Because a job's exit status alone does not explain why a measurement is missing, the record must also log which metric was censored and why: a place-and-route job that hits its timeout has a known compute and license cost, even though its final routed wirelength remains unknown (right-censored).

| **Evaluation attribute group** | **Attributes added or made explicit for comparison** |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Comparison placement** | Comparison arm, paired task, workflow-run/candidate/configuration/attempt identifiers, random seed where applicable, evaluator-owned stage/fidelity, and promotion status |
| **Engineering outcome** | Passed, violated, infeasible, inconclusive, or unreached; coverage, waiver status, and deepest evidence stage |
| **Execution, censoring, and disposition** | Completed, crashed, timed out, canceled, or license unavailable; allocated timeout; censored measurement and reason, if any; partial output; and inclusion rules |
| **Resources and cost** | Model/tool calls; core-hours, accelerator-hours, peak memory, storage, network, energy, license occupancy duration and peak concurrency, queue wait latency, backoff throttling status, retries, and recovery |
| **Recovery and state** | State invalidated/restored, preserved descendants, and checkpoint lineage |
| **Human-work linkage** | Active engineering minutes by role, independent review, intervention, and waiting linked to affected attempts |
: **Evaluation records extend operational tracking across all attempts.** Capturing outcomes, censoring, resource consumption, and linked human effort across all attempts prevents artificial cost erasure from finalist-only reporting. {#tbl-attempt-cost-record tbl-colwidths="[30,70]"}

### Counting Compute, Licenses, Engineering Hours, and Amortization {#sec-resource-vectors-amortization}

Because senior architect hours, GPU hours, commercial EDA license hours, and calendar delays are not interchangeable commodities, a rigorous cost study reports them as a multi-element resource vector rather than collapsing them into a single arbitrary score. Whenever a study converts those resources into dollars, it must state the currency, base year, and pricing rates used. The record must also separate active resource demand (CPU core-hours, peak memory, active tool runtime, and checked-out license hours) from calendar delay (queue wait times, license-denial stalls, and cluster preemptions). Running fifty simulations in parallel cuts wall-clock time without reducing total CPU core-hours, whereas sitting in a congested license queue stretches wall-clock schedule without burning extra CPU cycles; both numbers matter to an engineering manager, and each answers a different question.

Observed run costs, one-time setup or model-training overhead, and projected future maintenance costs must remain separate in the tables, under a stated amortization horizon and identical accounting rules for both comparison arms. For an additive resource such as engineering hours, a fixed setup cost $F$ shared across $N$ design tasks adds $F/N$ per task on top of the direct per-task work, whereas non-additive limits such as peak memory footprint and peak simultaneous license checkouts must be reported directly as maxima. Because an assumed reuse count $N$ is a projection rather than a measured fact, the study should report the unamortized fixed cost $F$ and show how the per-task comparison shifts across realistic values of $N$, making the break-even horizon clear.

A candidate's maintainability and future ECO difficulty also must stay separate from the hours already spent during the study: an estimate of how hard a generated module will be to patch later is a property of the candidate artifact, whereas the hours an engineer actually spent performing an ECO test during the experiment belong in the observed workflow cost. Keeping those records linked but distinct prevents double-counting, just as reporting upfront setup cost either once for the whole campaign or amortized as $F/N$ per task prevents charging both the lump sum and the per-task share at the same time.

With these accounts in place, a study can evaluate two distinct kinds of efficiency: *complete-workflow efficiency*, which measures the hardware quality achieved per unit of total human and machine budget, and *sample efficiency*, which measures how much a search method improves candidate quality per tool evaluation at a given fidelity. A learned optimizer that finds a good floorplan in half as many place-and-route runs is more sample-efficient, but if training its surrogate and curating its dataset consumed more GPU time and engineer hours than the saved place-and-route jobs, its complete-workflow efficiency may still be worse. Evaluations must state clearly which tool calls enter the sample-efficiency denominator while keeping all remaining training, generation, checking, and human review costs in the complete-workflow account, and both metrics must account for run-to-run variance across seeds [@BouthillierEtAl2021UnreproducibleML; @HendersonEtAl2018DeepRL].

### Tracking Candidate Attrition Across Evaluation Stages {#sec-candidate-flow-funnels}

To see where those attempt costs go across a search campaign, candidate identity must be tracked by what the design actually is rather than by batch-job IDs. When a workflow edits an RTL module or changes a cache parameter to fix a failure, that semantic change creates a new child candidate linked to its parent; when the harness simply reruns the exact same RTL after a license server stall or a container crash, the retry keeps the same candidate ID and logs a new attempt under it. Tracking parent–child links alongside retry attempts lets an evaluation distinguish genuine exploration of new designs from local patching and mechanical retries, showing whether a thousand logged jobs explored a thousand distinct architectures or merely repaired three templates over and over.

Reporting only the winning candidate hides how many designs failed along the way and how much each filtering stage cost. Grouping all execution attempts by candidate ID produces a per-arm candidate funnel (@tbl-candidate-funnel) that counts each unique candidate once at the deepest evaluation stage it reaches while summing the cost of every attempt spent on it. The funnel shows exactly where candidates drop out and why, separating designs that violated a physical constraint, designs that were healthy but outranked during pruning, and designs whose verification jobs timed out or crashed. If no candidates reach a given stage, the table reports a count of zero and marks the stage pass fraction as undefined rather than dividing by zero.

| **Funnel stage** | **Count and fractions to report per arm** | **Required denominators** | **Linked attrition and cost accounting** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Unique candidates proposed** | Count $U$; starting fraction $U/U$ | All unique candidates proposed or supplied to the arm | Proposal cost, duplicate attempts, and candidates censored before eligibility review |
| **Low-fidelity eligibility** | Count $E$; $E/U$ | All unique candidates proposed | Eligibility outcome, attrition reason, stage cost, retries, and censoring |
| **Promoted or finalist** | Count $P$; $P/E$ and $P/U$ | Eligible candidates and all unique candidates proposed | Promotion rule, nonpromotion reasons, selection cost, ties, and retries |
| **Higher-fidelity completion** | Count $H$; $H/P$ and $H/U$ | Promoted candidates and all unique candidates proposed | Completed check identity, noncompletion reasons, stage cost, timeouts, and infrastructure failures |
| **Blocking-check pass** | Count $B$; $B/H$ and $B/U$ | Higher-fidelity completions and all unique candidates proposed | Blocking-check identity, pass/violation/waiver status, stage cost, and retries |
| **Final comparison and selection** | Counts $C$ compared, $S$ selected; $C/B$, $S/C$, $S/U$ | Blocking-check passes, final comparison set, and all unique candidates proposed | Comparison/selection rule, dominated/unselected reasons, final-stage cost, and declared no-selection outcomes |
: **Candidate funnels expose stage-by-stage attrition and resource consumption.** Counts, fractions, denominators, reasons, retries, censoring events, and stage costs remain connected to attempt lineage rather than reported only for finalists. {#tbl-candidate-funnel tbl-colwidths="[22,26,24,28]"}

A candidate that passes cheap linting and cycle simulation only to fail post-route timing tells a very different story from a candidate whose place-and-route job was killed when the compute budget ran out. Keeping those exit reasons separate in the funnel prevents finalist-only reporting from hiding both the rejected designs and the compute burned on candidates that never finished verification.

Stage costs in the funnel are summed from the underlying attempt records, counting shared human engineering sessions once across the attempts they supported and recording the stage reached, check name, outcome, total cost, verification coverage, and any approved waivers alongside the headcounts. Analytical models, cycle simulators, formal property proofs, equivalence checks, synthesis runs, place-and-route flows, and lab silicon measurements remain separate observation classes in the funnel, each carrying its own cost and supporting its own level of claim (@sec-feedback-verification-trust).

### Cost-Quality Frontiers {#sec-cost-quality-frontiers}

Investing compute in learned surrogates or guided search upfront pays off when it cuts downstream tool failures or uncovers better microarchitectural trade-offs [@Kahng2018Machine]. Whether that investment is worthwhile on a real project depends on the bottom line of the comparison: delivering a better verified design within the same total budget, matching the baseline's hardware quality at lower total cost, or achieving both. Saving human architect and verification-engineer hours counts as a genuine gain even if the final chip PPA and tool crash rates match the conventional flow. An evaluation harness must therefore plot each verified candidate's architectural quality against the total cost spent to reach it, tracing the empirical cost-quality Pareto frontier of nondominated outcomes.

A candidate sits on that nondominated frontier only if no other candidate achieves equal or better hardware quality at equal or lower cost with at least one strict improvement. Because a frontier is only as honest as its axes, the cost and quality axes must state whether they plot physical measurements or cheap proxies: an area figure calculated by multiplying a fixed constant per processing element and per kilobyte of static random-access memory (SRAM) is an analytical model estimate, not a post-route silicon area, and the resulting frontier remains a proxy curve until backed by physical implementation. Where quality gains flatten out at the high-cost end of the curve, a predeclared acceptance threshold, locked in before candidates are ranked, picks the lowest-cost design that meets the project's target and drops larger configurations whose marginal gains are not worth the extra die area or compute bill. And because the line segments drawn between discrete points on a Pareto plot are visual guides rather than buildable hardware designs, every selected point must pass its own structural and timing signoff checks before it can be admitted.

Plotting a cost-quality frontier shows how efficiently an AI-native system trades compute and engineering time for hardware quality within its own runs. Proving that the frontier beats existing engineering practice, however, requires holding it up against a strong external competitor under matched conditions.

## Matched Baseline and Candidate Comparisons {#sec-matched-baseline-comparisons}

Choosing that competitor requires care, because an isolated performance gain or synthesis score cannot show on its own whether an AI-native workflow improves on a strong alternative. Consider a heavily tuned, prompt-engineered AI-native search loop compared with an untuned commercial EDA default or a naive random search: if the AI-native loop receives hundreds of exploration iterations while the conventional baseline gets only a single run, a better result could reflect unequal tuning opportunities rather than a superior workflow. Because the comparison must make those opportunities and their costs visible, selecting a baseline that fits the claim and establishing matched test conditions are part of the evaluation itself.

### Matching Protocols and Comparator Baselines {#sec-matching-protocols-comparators}

Giving an AI-native search loop hundreds of compute-hours and tuned hyperparameters while running a conventional EDA baseline once with out-of-the-box defaults can manufacture an artificial win, as the dispute over learned macro placement illustrates: the original study compared a learned placer against baselines configured by its authors [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement], those authors defended their setup against skeptics [@GoldieEtAl2024ThatChipHasSailed], and an updated assessment running commercial and academic placers as comparators reached different conclusions [@ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment]. Whichever reading one finds persuasive, the disagreement turns largely on what each arm was allowed to tune and at what cost. When a team claims that a complete workflow deserves adoption, the evaluation has to test whether that workflow improves supported architecture outcomes or lowers total cost relative to the strongest practical alternative across declared tasks, conditions, budgets, and checks. Both workflows must therefore be matched across the architecture questions they answer, the starting artifacts and tools they can access, the evaluator-owned checks they must pass, and the cost rules, budgets, and stopping criteria that govern each run.

Within those matched rules, different comparison arms test different questions: random search tests whether guided search beats unguided sampling under the same budget; a conventional workflow paired with point AI assistance tests whether a narrow helper improves on current practice; and comparisons across no-AI, retrieval-only, foundation-model, and full AI-native configurations show how their supported outcomes and total costs differ. These configurations need not form a steady progression of capability. Random search is useful as a diagnostic floor, though whether it also counts as a credible practical alternative depends on the architecture problem, where the real competition may instead be direct enumeration, deterministic heuristics, commercial optimizers, established EDA flows, or human-directed studies (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization).

Once the comparator is chosen, holding the dimensions in @tbl-matched-system-comparison fixed rules out alternative explanations for a measured gain, while any differences that cannot be matched must remain explicit limits on the comparison.

| **Comparison element** | **Matching rule** |
| --- | --- |
| **Evaluation object** | Compare complete workflows for adoption estimates; reserve components for controlled ablations. |
| **Architecture question** | Require both workflows to resolve the same design decision under matched conditions; retain the identities of the distinct candidates each produces. |
| **Starting information** | Provide identical specifications, artifacts, workload info, prior results, and source access. |
| **Development and tuning** | Grant comparable opportunity, expertise, and budget for prompt, heuristic, and workflow tuning. |
| **Evaluation tools and checks** | Provide identical evaluator-run tools and stages, judged by identical evaluator-owned checks. |
| **Budget** | Enforce a single cost-accounting window across declared human, machine, tool, review, and time budgets. |
| **Human capability** | Deploy practitioners with matched task expertise in both arms and record specific actions. |
| **Human-judged outcomes** | Conceal arm identities and randomize review order wherever artifacts permit. |
| **Stopping rule** | Apply identical success, failure, exhaustion, and timeout conditions across both arms. |
| **Reporting** | Publish symmetric architecture outcomes, failed runs, costs, and uncertainty profiles. |
: **A matched comparison holds the architecture task and evidence standard fixed.** Matching reduces alternative explanations; remaining differences limit the resulting estimate of complete-workflow effects. {#tbl-matched-system-comparison tbl-colwidths="[26,74]"}

Put together, those rules run two complete workflows side by side on one frozen study (@fig-matched-complete-systems).

![**Matched complete-system workflows bound the net effect of AI-native adoption.** Holding the architecture question, starting artifacts, and verification tools invariant across parallel arms isolates workflow-level advantages. Differences in supported outcomes and total cost quantify whole-system adoption effects without attributing credit to isolated algorithmic components.](images/fig-matched-complete-systems){#fig-matched-complete-systems
fig-alt="Flow diagram in which one declared architecture study feeds an AI-native complete human-plus-technical workflow and the strongest practical complete workflow, while fixing the architecture question, starting artifacts and source access, shared evaluation tools, evaluator-owned acceptance checks, conditions, cost-accounting window, budgets, stopping rules, and reporting requirements. Each workflow returns a supported architecture outcome or declared failure, stated limits, a resource-cost record, and results across repeated runs and varied conditions, with failed runs retained in the reported results. Task-paired differences estimate the effect of adopting the whole AI-native workflow conditional on matching assumptions and the tested envelope rather than isolating a single component or AI contribution."
width="80%"}

The paired difference this side-by-side design yields is deliberately coarse: because it charges the AI-native arm for its prompt tuning, model inferences, and hand-written wrapper code while charging the comparator for its own tuning and triage, it answers whether adopting one whole workflow instead of the other pays off. It cannot say whether a generative model or a heuristic rule inside the winning arm drove the outcome; separating those contributions requires controlled component ablation (@sec-locating-component-contribution).

### Predeclaration and the Confirmation Firewall {#sec-predeclaration-confirmation-firewall}

Without predeclared decision rules, post hoc analysis can easily reclassify a trivial $0.5\%$ IPC bump as a success, celebrate lower run costs when architecture quality has degraded, or report the best of twenty prompt-tuning trials as if it were a held-out test. Before either arm begins confirmatory runs, the evaluation protocol must therefore predeclare the primary architecture outcomes, required task and condition coverage, acceptable total-cost envelopes, and minimum thresholds for a worthwhile improvement in architecture quality or cost. It must also set a strict ceiling on acceptable quality loss and specify the number of paired tasks and statistical repeats needed to distinguish those margins with confidence.

Fixing those decision thresholds goes hand in hand with fixing the task population in the study plan, which names the exact class of architecture decisions the program claim covers and defines how tasks, workloads, implementation conditions, and repeats are sampled from that class. Because adaptive prompt development, method tuning, and search-heuristic exploration must stay confined to a designated development set, primary workflow comparisons require held-out tasks and conditions that never influenced design choices, followed by evaluator-owned confirmation of any selected architecture result.

That boundary acts as a confirmation firewall between exploratory development and confirmatory testing [@NosekEtAl2018Preregistration]: the study record logs how many prompts, models, routing policies, metrics, task variants, and analysis techniques were tried before settling on the final configuration, and names the primary outcome and planned analysis before the holdout set is inspected. Whenever adaptive searching across configurations or metrics could plausibly explain a reported advantage, the study needs a fresh confirmation set rather than treating the best development run as confirmatory evidence [@DworkEtAl2015ReusableHoldout]. This same development opportunity and accounting rule apply to the strongest practical alternative, so when a mature baseline carries decades of inherited engineering refinement, the study records that historic advantage rather than tuning only the AI-native arm and declaring the contest matched.

Human participation across the two arms requires similar controls, starting with a predeclared balancing or randomization rule that logs who worked on which task. If the same architect operates both systems, the protocol rotates tool order and reports order effects while recognizing that rotation alone cannot erase design knowledge acquired in an earlier run; if different engineering teams are deployed, their experience is matched and remaining skill gaps are reported. Both arms also receive a declared familiarization period and stable operating procedure, with setup time logged separately from active task duration but retained in total-cost accounting. Whenever exposure to the first arm reveals design insights that would help on the second, the study either switches to fresh tasks where those insights do not apply or reports the carryover as an explicit limit, since a waiting period or carryover model requires a task-specific justification and elapsed time alone never erases what an architect has already learned.

Human judgment also enters when reviewers grade qualitative outcomes such as RTL maintainability or explanation quality, so arm labels are concealed and review order is randomized wherever feasible. Because generated artifacts often give away their origin through distinct coding styles or structural quirks, the study records any leaked cues, unblinded judgments, reviewer agreement rates, and final adjudication rules.

Once confirmatory runs begin, every assigned run must stay in the final result pool. Runs that return an incomplete design, hit a timeout, suffer a tool failure, or exhaust their compute budget keep both their declared status and the resources they consumed, rather than quietly disappearing from the denominator because they produced no final benchmark score. While summaries restricted to successful runs can offer a useful secondary view of peak quality, they cannot replace the all-assigned comparison on which the workflow adoption claim depends.

How the analysis treats a timeout within that pool depends on the question under test. When the targeted outcome is succeeding within a fixed budget, a timeout counts directly as a failure; when the metric is the time required to reach a supported result, the timeout is a right-censored observation whose true completion time is known only to exceed the cutoff (@sec-data-representations-world-models) [@KleinMoeschberger2003Survival]. In neither case may the analysis discard the timed-out run or plug in an invented completion time to simplify the math.

Retaining every run and its cost allows the evaluation to compare the cost-quality frontiers of both arms across predeclared budget milestones (@sec-cost-quality-frontiers). As human effort, model compute, tool utilization, and wall-clock time accumulate, the report tracks both the best supported architecture outcome at each milestone and the total cost needed to cross the declared quality threshold, enforcing the study's resource envelopes and conversion rules. Even a clear win on that whole-workflow frontier, however, leaves open which element inside the winning workflow actually produced the gain.

## Isolating Which Component Produced the Gain {#sec-locating-component-contribution}

While a matched baseline study estimates the net effect of adopting an entire workflow, finding out which component or method drove a gain requires controlled replacements and ablations. An ablation swaps or removes one element while holding the surrounding components, human procedures, task definitions, verification checks, and declared resource constraints fixed. Because generation, prediction, optimization, and coordination are selectable method families rather than mandatory stages in every flow, the substitutions in @tbl-system-ablations test only the specific functions the workflow uses, asking which parts the outcome depends on without assuming that component contributions add independently.

| **Component under test** | **Useful comparison** | **Claim the comparison can support** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Complete AI-native workflow | Compare with the strongest practical alternative workflow under the same task, evidence standard, and total-cost accounting | The effect of adopting the whole workflow on result quality or cost, not an isolated AI contribution |
| Foundation model | Replace it with retrieval-only assistance, a smaller model, or another declared model while preserving the surrounding workflow | Whether the measured result depends on that model capability and its cost |
| Generation | Replace generated candidates with the same-size human, rule-based, or existing candidate set | Whether generation changed candidate quality or diversity at the declared cost |
| Prediction | Remove the learned screen or replace it with a conventional proxy and send a matched sample to the higher-fidelity check | Whether prediction saved evaluation work without discarding decisive candidates |
| Optimization | Replace the search policy with the strongest practical conventional method at matched budgets | Whether the optimizer improved the cost-quality relationship |
| Retrieved design information | Remove, freeze, or substitute the retrieval source while preserving the remaining system; check source versions, decision-relevant coverage, conflicts, and local claim support | Whether retrieved material changed results and which source dependencies remain |
| Routing and role selection | Replace adaptive routing with a fixed sequence or evaluator-declared component choice | Whether dynamic method and tool selection improved decisions or merely added complexity |
| Tool feedback | Restrict or delay selected feedback attributes while keeping tool stages fixed | Which returned information enables correction and which merely adds cost |
| Automated checking | Replace one checker with an independently developed check where feasible | Whether the conclusion depends on one checker or one shared assumption |
| Human intervention | Compare declared intervention policies and record every intervention | How much human work is necessary for the measured result |
: **Ablations locate dependencies inside a complete workflow.** They do not turn an interacting system architecture into a set of independent, additive contributions. {#tbl-system-ablations tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

Each comparison in @tbl-system-ablations sets its resource constraint to match the hypothesis under test: comparing architecture quality at a fixed budget gives every variant the same declared resource envelope, whereas comparing the cost of reaching a declared quality threshold runs variants under common stopping rules and accounts for every human, model, and tool resource spent, since equal tool-call counts alone never establish equal total cost. Whatever the budget rule, replacing one element at a time estimates that component's effect only within the tested configuration. A learned surrogate may help only when paired with a particular simulated-annealing optimizer, and a foundation model may look effective only because a human engineer catches its out-of-distribution errors before they reach Innovus. An ablation study therefore starts with the components most likely to drive the observed gains, tests targeted pairs when conclusions shift across configurations, and leaves individual contributions unresolved whenever the comparisons cannot separate coupled dependencies.

When a workflow combines dozens of prompts, surrogates, heuristics, and scripts across a large design space, testing every combination is impractical, so preregistered fractional-factorial experiments screen a balanced subset of configurations first. A Plackett–Burman design provides an efficient initial screen of main effects [@PlackettBurman1946Design],[^fn-plackett-burman-c10] followed by targeted runs to untangle specific high-value interactions before promising component combinations undergo held-out confirmation on evaluator-owned architectural benchmarks. Because fractional screens can confound main effects with interactions, an apparent single-component benefit may still depend on which other components were present, leaving untested or inseparable interactions unresolved, just as a single ablation run leaves open whether the measured advantage will hold up across repeated trials and shifting operating conditions.

[^fn-plackett-burman-c10]: **Plackett–Burman design**: A class of fractional-factorial experimental designs that screens $K$ main effects using only $N$ runs (where $N$ is a multiple of 4, $N > K$), rather than the $2^K$ runs demanded by full-factorial exploration. It assumes two-factor and higher-order interactions are negligible, enabling efficient linear scaling when identifying decisive workflow components.

## Testing Whether the Gain Survives Tool Noise and New Workloads {#sec-reliability-of-advantage}

Even when a matched comparison and its ablations show a clear gain in quality or cost, a single stochastic run supplies only a point observation without establishing that the advantage is repeatable [@HendersonEtAl2018DeepRL]. Repeated runs on the same task test whether an effect recurs under fixed conditions, whereas runs across varied conditions test whether the advantage survives practical shifts in workloads, constraints, or tool settings. Because same-task repeatability does not establish stability across changed conditions, extending a reliability claim to a new setting requires fresh evidence there, just as a transfer claim does.

A credible reliability record also looks past average pass rates to examine how badly the workflow fails and what recovery costs. Alongside mean performance, it tracks worst-case outcomes, blocking constraint violations, the fraction of automated decisions overridden by experts, and the human and machine time required to recover after a failure. Confidence estimates must also calibrate with actual architectural outcomes: a workflow that succeeds $90\%$ of the time but reports maximum confidence during its failures poses a worse risk to an engineering team than one with the same pass rate and well-calibrated uncertainty estimates.

When a surrogate or predictor returns numerical PPA estimates rather than binary pass/fail labels, calibration must be checked on those intervals directly. The evaluation reports empirical interval coverage, interval sharpness (keeping intervals narrow without sacrificing coverage), and error rates near decision boundaries [@GneitingRaftery2007ScoringRules, pp. 369, 374], each tied to specific tool stages, prediction horizons, and condition distributions. Because calibration measured on one workload, process node, design family, or toolchain cannot be assumed to hold once conditions shift [@OvadiaEtAl2019UncertaintyShift], moving to a new target setting requires remeasuring interval coverage and boundary error on those target cases, which qualifies predictor uncertainty under the new condition without proving that a proposed design is functionally correct or physically manufacturable.

### Separating Workflow Variance from EDA Tool Noise {#sec-system-apparatus-variance}

Routine jitter in synthesis scripts and placement seeds can swing mapped area or timing slack by $10\%$ to $30\%$, easily dwarfing a claimed $4\%$ architectural improvement whenever tool noise is not separated from workflow variance. Separating repeatable workflow gains from that run-to-run noise requires pairing comparison arms across tasks, controlled tool factors, and declared starting conditions while keeping clear what each source of variation represents. Varying a model or search seed produces repeated runs under a single fixed system configuration, whereas changing a prompt creates an altered system configuration unless a predeclared prompt-sampling policy is part of the system under test. Neither variation creates an independent architecture task, so the experimental-unit distinctions in @sec-minimum-complete-workflow-protocol govern what these repeats can establish.

Within a single task, repeated runs are where the generator's own dispersion is measured, since a single proposal that happened to win says nothing about the distribution it was drawn from. The evaluation therefore reports the full distribution of candidate quality alongside the fraction of candidates that violate declared constraints, supplemented by two diagnostics for diversity and prompt sensitivity: the fraction of proposals across repeated samplings that are unique legal configurations rather than duplicates, and whether a meaning-preserving rewording of the prompt preserves the ranking of candidates common to both runs (which acts as a configuration-sensitivity test whenever prompt sampling does not belong to the fixed system definition).
